hook_text: A map of your school and a map of Africa can be exactly the same size. So how do you know what is near and what is far?
clip_script: Every map is the world shrunk down, and the scale tells you how much. On a school plan, one centimetre might be ten metres. On a map of Africa, one centimetre might be two hundred kilometres. Same centimetre, totally different distance. Now the twist that confuses everyone: the school plan is a large-scale map. Why? Because things on it look large. You can see every classroom. The map of Africa is small-scale: whole cities shrink to dots. And here is a pro tip. Photocopy a map bigger, and a scale written in words becomes wrong. But a line scale, the little ruler printed on the map, grows with it. That is why your phone's map always shows a scale bar.
visual_style: A whiteboard split screen with a school plan and a map of Africa the same size; a one-centimetre bracket on each labelled 10 m and 200 km; a photocopier enlarging a map while the bar scale stretches with it.
